items.title: Joining a sports centre
lines: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help you?
Hi. I'd like to become a member, please. Can I do that over the phone?
Yes, of course. I just need to take a few details. Could I have your surname first?
Thank you. And your first name?
It's 14 Mill Lane. That's in Westbury.
Mill Lane, Westbury. And a contact phone number?
Let me read that back: 07734 812 659. Lovely. Now, which type of membership are you interested in? We have standard, off-peak and family.
I think off-peak. I work in the evenings, so I'd mostly come during the day.
That's fine. Off-peak means you can use the centre before 4 p.m. on weekdays. It costs 32 pounds a month.
Oh, I was told it was 28.
It was 28 until January, but it's gone up, I'm afraid. It's 32 now.
OK, no problem. Does that include the swimming pool?
Yes, the pool and the gym are included. Classes like yoga are extra, though, 4 pounds each.
Right. And when could I start?

You'll need to do an induction first, where a trainer shows you how to use the equipment safely. The next free session is on Thursday the 9th... sorry, no, that one's full. The next free one is Friday the 10th, at half past ten.
Great. Please bring some photo identification with you, like a passport or a driving licence, so we can make your membership card.
Will a student card be OK?
No, it needs to be an official document, I'm afraid. And one more thing: how did you hear about us?
Wonderful. That means you get your first month half price. Is there anything else?
Is there somewhere to leave my bike?
Yes, there's a cycle rack next to the main entrance. You'll need your own lock, though.

items.title: Booking a day tour
lines: Hello, Coastline Tours. This is Emma speaking.
Hello. I'm calling about your day trips. I'd like to book one for next week.
Certainly. Which tour were you thinking of?
The one to the castle and the lighthouse.
That's our most popular one. It runs on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Which day would suit you?
OK. And how many people is that for?
Two adults and one child. My son is nine.
Children under twelve pay half price, so that's 45 pounds for each adult and 22 pounds 50 for your son.
That's fine. What time does it leave?
The coach leaves at 8.15 from outside the train station. Please be there ten minutes early.
Outside the train station. Got it. Is lunch included?
Lunch isn't included, but the coach stops in a fishing village where there are several cafés. Many people bring a picnic, though.
Comfortable shoes are essential, because there are quite a lot of steps at the lighthouse. And it can be windy, so bring a jacket.
OK. What else do you need from me?
Just a name for the booking and an email address. What name is it?
Oh, of course. It's Mrs Okafor. O-K-A-F-O-R.
Thank you, Mrs Okafor. And an email address for the tickets?
Lovely. If you need to cancel, please tell us at least 48 hours before, and you'll get a full refund.

items.title: A guide to Greenway Park
items.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Greenway Park. My name's Tom, and I'm one of the volunteers here. Before you set off, I'd like to tell you a little about the park and show you where things are on the map. The park opened in 1998 on the site of an old brick factory, and since then it has grown to cover almost forty hectares. Most of the work is done by volunteers like me. In fact, we only have three paid members of staff. People often ask how the park is funded. Some money comes from the local council, but the largest part comes from donations from visitors, so please do use the boxes near the gates. This year, our main project has been the wildlife pond. We've been removing plants that don't belong here and adding native ones, and we've already seen more frogs and dragonflies than last summer. Next spring, we're hoping to build a new adventure playground, although that depends on getting permission from the council. Now, let's look at the map. We're standing at the main gate, at the bottom of the map. If you walk straight ahead along the main path, the first building on your left is the visitor centre, where you can pick up leaflets. Just past the visitor centre, on the same side, you'll find the toilets. The café is further along the main path, on the right, opposite the toilets. It has a lovely terrace overlooking the lake. If you carry on to the end of the main path, you'll reach the lake itself, which takes up most of the top of the map. The wildlife pond I mentioned is not by the lake, as people often expect. It's in the bottom right-hand corner of the park, behind the car park. And finally, the picnic area is in the top left corner, between the woods and the lake. Please remember that barbecues are only allowed there. Right, enjoy your visit.

items.title: Volunteering at a music festival
items.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information session. I'm Karen Doyle, and I coordinate the volunteers at the Riverside Music Festival. This will be our twelfth festival, and last year we had just over three hundred volunteers. Without them, the festival simply couldn't happen. First, some practical points. The festival runs for three days, from Friday the eighteenth to Sunday the twentieth of July. We ask every volunteer to work at least two shifts of six hours. In return, you get a free ticket for the whole weekend, meals during your shifts, and a festival T-shirt, which you must wear while you're working, so that visitors can recognise you. A lot of people ask about camping. Volunteers can stay at the staff campsite free of charge, but you need to bring your own tent. The campsite is quieter than the main one, although I can't promise you'll get much sleep! Training is compulsory. There's a two-hour session on Saturday the twelfth of July at the community hall. If you can't make that date, there's an online version, but you must complete it at least three days before the festival starts. Now, let me tell you about the different teams. The information team works in the tents near each entrance, answering questions and handing out maps. You don't need any experience, but you do need to be patient, because people ask the same questions all day. The stewarding team manages crowds near the stages. This is the only team where we ask for previous experience, because safety is involved. The recycling team collects and sorts rubbish around the site. It's hard physical work, but people say it's the most fun. The artist team looks after the performers backstage, and that involves working late, often until two in the morning. And finally, the children's area team runs games and craft activities. Everyone in that team needs a police check, which we arrange for you, but it takes around four weeks, so please apply early. Applications close at the end of this month.
opts: B involves working late at night
D needs a lot of patience
F is the most popular team

items.title: Volunteering at a community centre
items.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming to this welcome session for new volunteers. My name's Sarah Okafor, and I'm the manager here at Westbury Community Centre. As most of you know, the centre has just reopened after eight months of building work. The old building was more than fifty years old, and the main problem was the heating, which broke down almost every winter. So the biggest change is one you won't actually see: a completely new heating system. We've also put in a lift, so every part of the building can now be reached by wheelchair users. Our opening hours have changed slightly. We used to stay open until nine in the evening, but so few people came in late that we now close at eight o'clock from Monday to Friday. At weekends we're open from ten until four, the same as before. Now, a word about what we'd like you to do. You won't need to deal with room bookings or payments, because the office staff look after all of that. Your main job is to welcome visitors and help them find the activity or room they've come for. On busy days, we may also ask you to help set out chairs in the main hall. Parking is a bit of a problem here. The small car park behind the centre is only for visitors with disabilities and for deliveries, so please use the public car park on Mill Street. It's free after six, but better still, come by bus or bike if you can. And if the fire alarm ever goes off, everyone should leave by the nearest door and meet on the grass area across the road. Please don't wait in the car park, because the fire engines need that space. Right, let's look at the plan of the ground floor. We're in the entrance area at the bottom of the plan, and reception is straight in front of you. Behind reception, a corridor runs all the way up to the main hall at the top. As you walk along the corridor, the first room on your left is the café. It's run by a local charity, and volunteers get a ten per cent discount. People often expect the first aid room to be next to reception, but in fact it's directly opposite the café, on the right-hand side of the corridor. Carry on along the corridor, and the next room on the left is the computer room, where we run free classes for older residents. The art studio can only be reached through the main hall. Go into the hall and you'll see a door on the right-hand side. The studio is through there, in the top right-hand corner of the building. And finally, if you're helping families, the children's play room is easy to find. As you come in through the entrance, turn right straight away, before you get to reception. It's in the bottom right-hand corner. OK, any questions so far?

qs.why: "a completely new heating system" và "We've also put in a lift"; giờ mở cửa ngắn lại (đóng 8 giờ thay vì 9), bãi xe vẫn nhỏ.

qs.why: Trước đây 9 giờ tối, nay "we now close at eight o'clock"; 4 giờ là giờ đóng cửa cuối tuần, 6 giờ là giờ bãi xe miễn phí.

items.title: Planning a project on urban gardens
lines: So, Liam and Sofia, you've chosen urban gardens for your group project. How's the planning going?
Quite well, I think. We've decided to focus on community gardens rather than private ones, because there's more research on them.
And because we can actually visit a couple of them here in the city.
Good. What's the main question you want to answer?
At first we wanted to look at how much food they produce, but that seemed too narrow.
So now we're asking what social benefits they bring to a neighbourhood.
That's a much better question. How are you going to collect data?

We were going to do an online questionnaire, but we realised the people who use the gardens are mostly older, and many of them don't go online much. So we're going to interview gardeners in person instead.
Sensible. Now, you sent me a list of sources. Let's go through them quickly. What did you think of the book by Martin?
It's really useful. It covers the history of community gardens in a lot of cities, so it'll be good for our introduction.
Honestly, it's a bit out of date. It's from 2009, and a lot has changed since then.
Fair enough, but you could still use it to show how things have changed. What about the article by Chen?
That one's quite hard to follow. It's full of statistics, and I'm not sure we understood all of it.
Come and see me if you need help with it. It's worth the effort. And the documentary?
We both loved it. It's very inspiring, but it only shows success stories, so I don't think it's very balanced.
Good point. And lastly, the city council website?
It's got a map of all the gardens in the city, so that's how we chose which ones to visit.
Excellent. When do you plan to do the interviews?
Probably in the first two weeks of next month. Most gardeners are there on Saturday mornings, so that's when we'll go.
And how will you divide the work?
Sofia's better at writing, so she'll write the report, and I'll do the interviews and the presentation slides.
Well, we'll both do the interviews, actually. But yes, I'll write most of the report.
opts: E helped them choose places to visit

items.title: Discussing a survey on students' sleep
lines: Come in, Tom and Hana. You wanted to talk about your survey on students' sleep?
Yes. We've collected the data, but we're not sure how to present it.
How many responses did you get in the end?
A hundred and twenty. We were hoping for two hundred, but it was exam season, so a lot of people didn't reply.
That's still a reasonable sample. What surprised you most?
I expected most students to sleep less than seven hours, and they did. What surprised me was how many said they slept badly even when they had time. Nearly half.
For me, the surprise was caffeine. I assumed coffee would be the main problem, but energy drinks were far more common than we thought.
Interesting. Did you ask about phones?
We did. But almost everyone uses their phone in bed, so we can't compare people who do and people who don't. We can't really say anything about the effect.
That's an honest conclusion, and it's better than claiming more than your data shows. Now, the presentation. What were you thinking?
I wanted to put all the results in one big table.
Tables are fine for the appendix, but in the talk you need something the audience can take in quickly.
Maybe a bar chart for sleep hours, and a pie chart for the drinks?
A bar chart, yes. But pie charts are hard to read when there are more than three or four categories. How many types of drink did you have?
Then I'd use bars for that too. And include a few quotations from the open questions. They bring the numbers to life.
We've got some great ones. One student said she drinks coffee to wake up and herbal tea to fall asleep.
Perfect. Now, what will you each do before Friday?
And I'll write the section on limitations: the sample size and the timing.
We'll do that together, since we both read all the answers.
And someone needs to check that nothing in the quotations could identify a student.
I'll do that. I've already removed the names from the data.
Good. And practise the talk at least twice.
I'll book a room so we can practise together on Thursday.

qs.q: Why did fewer students reply than expected?
qs.a: It was during the exam period.
qs.why: "it was exam season, so a lot of people didn't reply"

a: how many students slept badly even when they had time
w: how many students slept more than eight hours

items.title: Lecture: living things that make light
items.text: Today I'm going to talk about bioluminescence, which is the ability of living things to produce their own light. Most people have seen fireflies, but in fact the majority of bioluminescent species live in the ocean. Some scientists estimate that around three quarters of the animals in the deep sea can produce light. So how does it work? In almost all cases, the light is the result of a chemical reaction. A substance called luciferin reacts with oxygen, and this reaction is controlled by an enzyme. Interestingly, very little heat is produced, which is why it is sometimes called cold light. The colour of the light varies, but in the ocean it is usually blue, because blue light travels furthest through water. Why do animals produce light? There are several reasons. The first is to find food. The anglerfish, for example, has a glowing lure on its head, which attracts small fish towards its mouth. The second reason is defence. Some squid release a cloud of glowing liquid, which confuses predators and allows the squid to escape. A third reason is communication. Fireflies use patterns of flashes to attract a partner, and each species has its own pattern. Bioluminescence is also being used by humans. Researchers have used the genes involved to study diseases, because cells can be made to glow when a certain process is happening inside them. There has even been research into using glowing plants to light streets, although this is still at an early stage, and the light is not yet bright enough to be practical. Finally, bioluminescence can tell us about the health of the ocean. Some light-producing bacteria glow less when water is polluted, so they can be used as a simple test of water quality. That's all for today. Next week, we'll look at how animals see in the dark.

items.title: Lecture: kelp forests and sea otters
items.text: Good morning. Today I want to talk about one of the most productive habitats on the planet: kelp forests. Kelp is a type of large brown seaweed. It grows in cold, shallow water close to the coast, and in good conditions some species can grow up to half a metre in a single day. These underwater forests provide food and shelter for thousands of species, from tiny snails to fish and seals. Kelp forests also matter to humans. They protect coastlines by reducing the energy of waves during storms, and they support important fisheries. More recently, scientists have become interested in their role in storing carbon, although how much carbon kelp actually stores in the long term is still debated. To understand how these forests stay healthy, we need to look at a small animal: the sea urchin. Urchins feed on kelp, and when there are too many of them, they can destroy a forest, leaving what scientists call an urchin barren: bare rock with almost nothing growing on it. This is where sea otters come in. Otters eat urchins. An adult otter needs to eat about a quarter of its body weight every day, because it has no layer of fat to keep it warm. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur. As otter numbers fell, urchin numbers rose, and large areas of kelp disappeared. Where otters have returned, the kelp has often recovered. Ecologists call an animal like this a keystone species: one whose effect on its environment is far greater than its numbers would suggest. Today, kelp faces new threats, particularly warmer water. In northern California, for example, a marine heatwave, combined with the loss of a starfish that also eats urchins, led to the disappearance of most of the region's kelp. Restoration projects now include removing urchins by hand, with the help of volunteer divers.

qs.why: "in cold, shallow water close to the coast"

items.title: Lecture: why cities are hotter
items.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about urban heat islands: the reason why cities are often warmer than the countryside around them. On a summer night, the centre of a large city can be as much as ten degrees warmer than nearby farmland. There are three main causes. The first is materials. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat from the sun during the day and release it slowly at night. The second is the lack of plants. In the countryside, trees and fields cool the air as water evaporates from their leaves, but cities have far fewer green spaces. The third is waste heat from human activity: air conditioners, cars and factories all add heat to the air. Let's look at three cities that have tried different solutions. In Singapore, new buildings are expected to include green spaces, so many towers now have gardens on their roofs and walls. In Los Angeles, some streets have been coated with a light grey paint that reflects sunlight, and tests found the road surface was around six degrees cooler. And in Paris, the city has opened what it calls cool islands: parks that stay open late into the night during heatwaves. Why does this matter? Heat is not only uncomfortable. During heatwaves, hospital admissions rise, and older people are most at risk, particularly those who live alone. Hot nights are especially dangerous, because the body cannot recover from the heat of the day. Finally, a word about the future. Planners increasingly measure the temperature of every street using sensors on buses, which allows them to plant trees where they are needed most.
